prize_parts.citation: For the theory of defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase, showing how dislocation unbinding controls phase transitions in two-dimensional matter.

statement.case_for: B020 is the cleanest example on the shortlist of what I look for: a simple, universal mechanism behind a messy many-body phenomenon. Halperin and Nelson (1978) and Young (1979) showed that melting in two dimensions can proceed in two continuous steps, dislocation unbinding followed by disclination unbinding, with an intermediate hexatic phase that has quasi-long-range orientational order and Kosterlitz-Thouless-type critical behaviour. The prediction was analytically tractable, it was falsifiable, and it was tested for decades in colloidal monolayers, liquid-crystal films, and simulations. The attribution is unusually clear, since the three theory authors are the decisive originators and the credited trio fits the three-person limit exactly. The 2016 prize recognised topological defects and phase transitions in the Kosterlitz-Thouless and Haldane context, and this work is the natural, still-unrecognised extension into soft and two-dimensional matter; it is also an old result whose authors should be honoured while they can be. I would cite it for the mechanism, not for any later application.
statement.case_against: I have to accept that no colleague other than me ranked B020, so on opening support it is the weakest-supported candidate among those I rank first. The argument against it is substantive as well: the 2016 prize may be seen as having already covered the topological-defect idea, the first-order versus continuous nature of 2D melting is not settled universally (it depends on the system, and the hexatic phase was established firmly only in particular colloidal and film systems), and a committee that favours discoveries which change what we can observe or measure may see this as a theoretical result with less visible impact on technology or on new instruments. Its age also invites the objection that it should have been recognised earlier.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B043) first, arguing that the magic-wavelength idea is simple, original and decisive, that Katori and Ye are a clean pair, and that independent confirmation across Sr, Yb and Hg is strong.
responses.response: I agree with most of this and it moved me: B043 is the most mature and best-attributed experimental candidate, and the magic-wavelength idea is exactly the sort of simple mechanism I respect. Where I qualify is the framing. Much of the case rests on applications, redshift geodesy, dark-matter searches, and a future redefinition of the second, that have not happened yet. The Hall and Hansch frequency-comb prize and the Wineland and Haroche prize already cover much of the precision-metrology ground, so I would want the citation to rest on the lattice-clock concept and its demonstrated 1e-18 performance, not on prospective applications. I would accept B043 as a strong, defensible outcome.

responses.point: Eriksson places twisted bilayer graphene (B029) first as theory and experiment fitting together quantitatively, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicting magic-angle flat bands and the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity.
responses.response: I share the high view of B029 and ranked it third; the prediction-then-observation structure is exactly what makes a theory credit convincing. My reservation is the one you mention yourself: the origin of the superconducting pairing is still debated, so we would be crowning a platform and a phenomenon rather than an understood mechanism, and the 2011 theory predates the 2018 experiment by seven years with the experimental credit contested between Cao and Jarillo-Herrero and other groups. Compared with B020, where the mechanism is understood, B029 is more recent and more exciting but less settled. I would put it ahead of B043 only if the committee is willing to reward a field before its central puzzle is resolved.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube (B010) first as a landmark of instrument building that opened neutrino astronomy, with Halzen and Karle as the decisive pair, and treats the 2013 diffuse flux plus the blazar, NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results as established.
responses.response: I accept that IceCube is a genuine new window and that the diffuse flux is robust. My difficulty is attribution, which several members flag including Danielsson and Kroll: a collaboration of hundreds, the AMANDA precursor, and the fact that the source picture rests on a handful of events. Choosing Halzen and Karle leaves out Yoshida and many others, and I cannot say what the essential physical mechanism is that the prize would honour. I do not dispute the discovery, but a two-person IceCube prize seems to me more arbitrary than the pair for B043 or the trio for B020. I would like to hear the case for why Halzen and Karle are decisive beyond leadership roles.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, calling the idea simple and original, trapping atoms so the light shift cancels, with clean two-name credit and many independent laboratories reproducing 1e-18 performance.
responses.response: I agree about the elegance of the magic-wavelength trick, and I accept that attribution to Katori and Ye is as clean as any on the list. I would push on whether the committee is weighing mature precision metrology more heavily than a conceptual advance in understanding. Both are legitimate Nobel categories, but we should not equate unanimity among the experimentalists on the committee with the strongest scientific case. I would also ask whether Ye's role is fairly captured as implementation of Katori's idea, given that his group also drove many-body clock physics and the comparison work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards 2D melting as already covered by the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize, and whether the first-order versus continuous debate in specific systems weakens the citation.
Whether any colleague outside me will support a purely theoretical statistical-physics prize when three experimental candidates (B043, B010, B029) have broader opening support.
How the credit for B029 should be divided among Cao, Jarillo-Herrero and other experimental groups, and whether a 2011 theory-plus-2018 experiment pairing is enough.
I am working from recollection of the literature, not verified sources, and the relative maturity of the hexatic evidence in experiment is the point I am least sure of.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the credited persons on any shortlisted ballot appears among my frequent co-authors or institutional connections. I am in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), but I know of no collaboration with them, and no shortlisted candidate touches my own work on turbulent aerosols.
